data.title: Unín – Zámčisko, a massive hillfort discovered by Janšák
data.excerpt: In the middle of a ridge north-east of Unín, nature formed a kind of stepped pyramid of earth that our ancestors turned into one of the finest hillforts in western Slovakia: a rampart 4 to 6 metres high combined with a ditch of 8 to 10 metres. Štefan Janšák discovered it in 1927, and its occupation runs from the Early Bronze Age through the Maďarovce–Věteřov culture to a brooch and Germanic sherds of the Early Roman period.

children.text: Zámčisko near Unín is one of the finest hillforts in western Slovakia, and its massive rampart defences can still be admired today.

It was built in the middle of a 2 km long ridge, north-east of the village of Unín. At one point, towards spot height 411, the ridge drops away abruptly and thus forms a mountain promontory suitable for founding a hillfort, which our ancestors duly made use of. Štefan Janšák, who discovered the hillfort in 1927, states that nature created here a kind of irregular, stepped pyramid of earth. Its summit plateau, almost entirely level, is bounded by an irregular egg-shaped curve lined with ramparts or with a steep slope, which creates an easily defensible fortified area measuring approximately 70 × 132 m. As at other hillforts, the rampart is highest at the points from which access to the hillfort was easiest, and in its most massive stretch it is 4 to 6 metres high, which is combined with a deep ditch of 8 to 10 metres. The hillfort covers an area of as much as 17 ha.

children.text: The website of the village states that the oldest part of the hillfort was evidently built as early as the Early and Middle Bronze Age (2000–1250 BC). It reached its peak in two phases, which ended in devastating plundering, as the charred remains discovered during the archaeological excavations prove. The first culminating culture was the Maďarovce–Věteřov culture, whose occupation of the hillfort falls in the years 1550–1530 BC. Members of this culture inhabited not only south-western Slovakia but also the adjoining areas of present-day Moravia and northern Austria. According to the archaeological finds, the type of occupation corresponded rather to the cultural development of the Maďarovce culture on the Moravian side than to that of the central area, which lay in south-western Slovakia. The inhabitants were excellent craftsmen, above all potters, although they did not know the potter's wheel. The dominant part of the whole hillfort complex was the acropolis. The overall defence was secured in several lines of defence. A triple network was set forward in the localities known as Ku klancu and K Brovištiam. In times of danger this space between the first and the second line of defence thus served as a refuge for the surrounding population. These defences, consisting of a stone-and-earth construction strengthened with wooden beams and an adjoining pointed ditch, represented an effective defence against enemies. From this period come finely beaten bronze daggers, bronze pins and dress fasteners, as well as the bronze hoard that was discovered, which contains buttons, mounts and bronze ornaments, so-called bosses, which were sewn onto clothing and had a protective function. I have not yet managed to obtain photographs or drawings of them.

The next inhabitants of the hillfort in the Middle Bronze Age (1450–1250 BC) were the people of the Middle Danube Tumulus culture. Unlike the previous inhabitants, they buried their dead under burial mounds, often with rich grave goods, above all of a military character. From this period archaeologists have managed to discover, for example, a fragment of a bronze spear and a bronze pendant of heart shape.

From the period of the Late Bronze Age (1250–1000 BC) it has not been possible to find a sufficient quantity of artefacts from which life at this hillfort could be reconstructed. We do know, however, that at the close of this phase the bearers of the Silesian–Platěnice culture (9th century BC) lived on the acropolis in an almost square sunken-featured building, and that they cremated their dead.

Zámčisko was continuously occupied until the Hallstatt period (750–450 BC), and isolated sherds of the Middle La Tène period (275–120 BC), when we come to the time of the Celts, suggest that Celtic occupation could have existed here too. The youngest finds revealed so far, in the form of a brooch, Germanic sherds and a complete vessel, come from the Early Roman period (0–180 AD), and they can be dated more precisely to the period 25–50 AD.

So far I have not been able to track down relevant information proving occupation of the hillfort in the Great Moravian period or in the Middle Ages. I recommend visiting the hillfort; you will even find an information panel there about the history of its occupation and excavation. A short distance from the hillfort there is an interesting lookout tower.
